title: Cbus urges crackdown on adviser fees
full_text:
Cbus chief executive Kristian Fok is urging the Albanese government to demand more clarity from financial advisers on the fees they charge superannuation accounts, following a $1 billion surge in charges over the period from 2023 to 2025.
In a letter to Assistant Treasurer Daniel Mulino on Friday, Fok said advice fees information should be collected and stored by regulators "to help identify high-risk advice models, platforms or deduction patterns" and be regularly assessed to ensure costs are reasonable and fair.
The letter landed days before Mulino delivers a highly anticipated speech to the National Press Club on Wednesday, where he is expected to reveal the political response to the $1 billion collapse of the Shield and First Guardian investment schemes.
The head of the $100 billion super fund welcomed the government's focus on tackling the "industrialised misselling" of super online, adding that the issues raised by the Shield and First Guardian failures had "highlighted how lead generation and referral networks can steer consumers towards complex investment strategies, with substantial advice fees often underpinning these distribution models".
The Cbus letter cited data showing total advice fees deducted from super accounts jumped by more than $1 billion from 2023 to 2025, while the growth rate in fees nearly tripled.
These Shield and First Guardian failures have cost thousands of unsuspecting victims their life savings, after they were lured by financial advisers and lead generators to transfer their super into a wealth management platform or a self-managed vehicle where their money was then directed into the two problematic schemes.
The schemes promised safe and diversified assets, which would provide higher returns than available at a traditional super fund, but liquidators and regulators have since found they actually held a grab-bag of risky illiquid assets propped up by questionable related-party transactions.
While super funds must disclose investment management costs, asset consulting costs, and other fee-related expenses, "advice fees associated with investment strategies are often not shown in a way that allows consumers, trustees, regulators or policymakers to assess their impact on long-term performance", Fok said.
Among Mulino's considerations in response to Shield and First Guardian is banning advice fee deductions from accounts where that advice leads to a member switching funds.
Fok's call for tougher policing on advice fees comes as industry super funds like Cbus are pushing for more leeway from government to offer financial advice to members.
Cbus, like many of its super fund peers, is losing the business of older, wealthier members to retail competitors and do-it-yourself options. Australian Prudential Regulation Authority data shows they lost $2 billion to rivals in the year to December 31. Lifting their advice offer is seen as a way to claw back some of that lost ground.
Fok said he was a supporter of quality financial advice, and that access to it "plays an important role in helping Australians make informed decisions about their retirement, manage risk and achieve better financial outcomes".
The conversation around advice - and super funds' role in providing it - has added a new dimension to Mulino's speech on Wednesday, given the 18-month wait for an overhaul to advice laws that would expand what they can provide members.
Big super's push for the reforms stepped up last week when the biggest pension provider, AustralianSuper, revealed it had hired Quality of Advice review chairwoman Michelle Levy as a director of a new advice-focused entity that would be used to roll out advice products to members.
Known as the Delivering Better Financial Outcomes package, the suite of changes would allow funds to proactively contact members and inform them of more appropriate investment options or account types.
It would also allow them to collectively charge all members for a greater range of intra-fund advice services, rather than a single member incurring bills in the thousands of dollars.
Yet advocacy group Super Consumers Australia has cautioned against giving super funds a greater role in advice, and pushed back on the industry's call for revisions to a best-interest duty, which requires a planner or fund to put a client's interest ahead of their own.
"Super funds are conflicted," said SCA chief executive Xavier O'Halloran. "They're incentivised to push people to their own products. This is why the consumer protections currently require advice to consider the broader needs of a consumer, including what other products on the market might best fit those needs.
"Obviously funds have no interest in doing this, so they are advocating for reforms which would see the best-interest duty watered down to the point that they wouldn't automatically have to consider people's broader interests or what products might better meet those needs outside of the fund."
While the changes would allow super funds to offer advice more cheaply and easily, O'Halloran argued what the sector was pushing for "ain't financial advice - it is sales."
